strengths: The paper targets an important limitation of conventional video anomaly detection: what counts as anomalous can depend on user requirements, policies, and deployment context. Language-conditioned definitions are a natural and potentially useful interface.
PreVAD is a substantial dataset contribution in scale and breadth, containing 35,279 videos, a hierarchical 35-category taxonomy, and anomaly descriptions.

The evaluation covers seven external datasets and includes a useful controlled comparison in which VadCLIP and LaGoVAD are both trained on PreVAD. The reported zero-shot detection improvements are generally consistent across datasets.

The model is reasonably simple, and the component ablations separately examine language guidance, dynamic video synthesis, negative mining, and the effect of PreVAD. weaknesses: The central claim—adaptation to changing anomaly definitions—is not convincingly evaluated. The quantitative experiments use one manually designed, dataset-specific category prompt and primarily measure ordinary cross-dataset zero-shot transfer. Actual label changes are demonstrated only through two qualitative examples. A convincing evaluation needs a benchmark with multiple conflicting definitions for the same videos, quantitative localization metrics under each definition, and tests involving category inclusion/exclusion, negation, paraphrases, and compositional definitions.

The conceptual treatment of concept drift is weak. The law-of-total-probability decomposition in Eq. 2 does not establish that drift is caused solely by P(Z|V), and conditioning on an observed definition does not by itself 'avoid' concept drift. P(Y|V,Z) may also change across environments. Moreover, a user-specified definition is better viewed as observed context or an intervention than as a latent variable conditioned on the video.

PreVAD appears to provide each video with labels under only one definition. It is therefore unclear how the training data supervise the claimed ability to reverse labels for the same event under alternative definitions. The paper needs a precise account of how definitions map to binary frame labels and what training examples teach the model exclusion or reversal semantics.

Potential train-test leakage is a major unresolved concern. PreVAD draws from public video-text datasets and web sources, while several evaluation datasets also consist of web videos. No duplicate or near-duplicate audit against the seven test datasets is reported. This is especially important given the large gains attributed to dataset scale.

The dataset construction and reproducibility information is insufficient in the submitted manuscript. The identities and versions of the MLLM, VLM, and LLM; prompts; acceptance thresholds; human annotation protocol; inter-annotator agreement; quality-audit sample sizes; and deduplication procedures are deferred or omitted. Code and data are only promised for future release.

Several comparisons confound model quality with substantially more training data. VadCLIP trained on PreVAD is the strongest controlled baseline, but broader comparisons often pit LaGoVAD trained on 35,279 videos against models trained on UCF-Crime or XD-Violence. Table 4's averaged detection score also mixes AP on XD-Violence with AUC on the other datasets, producing a quantity without a clear statistical interpretation. There are no multi-seed results, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

The loss presentation raises technical questions. The pseudo-label term in Eqs. 10–12 includes only the positive-label component and appears not to penalize false positives on pseudo-normal positions. The synthesis procedure, temporal labels after concatenation, MIL details, and unusual min-normal/max-abnormal inference rule are not specified sufficiently to assess or reproduce the method.

The paper does not adequately address privacy, surveillance misuse, demographic bias, exposure to violent material, licensing, or copyright. This is particularly concerning for a surveillance-oriented dataset assembled from web videos and public streams; criticizing movie copyright while not documenting licenses for the collected web data is inconsistent.

strengths: The paper identifies a practically relevant limitation of conventional video anomaly detection: what counts as anomalous can depend on user requirements, context, or policy, and natural-language conditioning is an intuitive interface for expressing such requirements.
PreVAD is potentially a valuable contribution due to its reported scale, domain coverage, hierarchical labels, and anomaly descriptions.

The reported zero-shot detection results are strong across seven established datasets. Training VadCLIP on PreVAD provides a useful partially controlled comparison showing that both the dataset and the proposed architecture contribute to performance.
The model is reasonably clear, and the ablations separately examine language guidance, dynamic video synthesis, and contrastive learning with negative mining.
weaknesses: The central claim is not convincingly evaluated. Almost all quantitative experiments measure ordinary cross-dataset zero-shot generalization under each dataset's fixed label definition, not adaptation when the same event changes between normal and abnormal definitions. Evidence for the claimed concept-drift capability consists essentially of two qualitative, potentially cherry-picked examples; there is no quantitative counterfactual benchmark varying definitions while holding videos fixed.

The probabilistic formulation does not substantiate the theoretical claims. Equation 2 is simply the law of total probability, and the assertion that concept drift is caused specifically by a change in P(Z|V) does not follow. A user-supplied definition is also better modeled as an observed conditioning variable or intervention than as a latent variable drawn conditionally on the video. Conditioning on Z may accommodate specified label changes, but it does not generally 'avoid concept drift.'

The language interface appears substantially less open-ended than advertised. The definition is represented as a dataset-specific category set containing a normal class and known anomaly classes, and evaluation uses manually designed prompts based on target-dataset class names. The paper does not test paraphrases, compositional rules, negation, unseen fine-grained definitions, conflicting definitions, prompt sensitivity, or arbitrary user policies.

There is a serious unaddressed risk of train-test contamination. PreVAD is collected from existing video-text datasets, YouTube/web material, streaming sources, and other recognition datasets, while evaluation datasets are also largely web-derived. No video-level or near-duplicate filtering against the seven test benchmarks is reported. This materially weakens the zero-shot claims.

Comparisons confound method quality with training-data scale and diversity. Most baselines are trained on much smaller UCF-Crime or XD-Violence sets, while LaGoVAD uses 35,279 videos. The same-data VadCLIP comparison helps, but only one architecture receives this control, leaving the broad state-of-the-art claim insufficiently isolated.

The ablations are too aggregated to explain the gains: they report averages rather than per-dataset results, variability over random seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical significance. They also do not isolate hard-negative mining from ordinary contrastive alignment or dynamic synthesis from simpler temporal augmentation and concatenation baselines.

Dataset quality is insufficiently validated. Annotation and filtering rely heavily on unspecified foundation models, yet the paper reports no systematic human audit, precision/recall of anomaly filtering, description faithfulness evaluation, inter-annotator agreement, demographic or geographic analysis, or label-noise estimates.

The paper provides no substantive discussion of privacy, consent, harmful surveillance applications, graphic content, demographic bias, or licensing and redistribution rights, despite collecting crime and surveillance videos from public web and camera sources.

Reproducibility is presently limited: data and code are only promised, while crucial implementation, prompting, annotation, deduplication, and baseline-reproduction details are deferred to supplementary material not included in the provided manuscript.

Some claims overstate the evidence. For example, ordinary cross-domain gains are said to confirm superiority in open-world scenarios, and the two qualitative examples are described as validating practicality. Classification is also mixed: on UCF-Crime, LaGoVAD improves accuracy over the PreVAD-trained VadCLIP baseline but lowers F1.

PreVAD is potentially a substantial resource: 35,279 videos, 11,979 abnormal examples, 35 subcategories, hierarchical labels, and anomaly descriptions represent a meaningful increase in scale and semantic annotation over standard VAD datasets.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for VAD, covering seven external datasets. LaGoVAD consistently improves over VadCLIP when both are trained on PreVAD, providing useful evidence that the architecture contributes beyond simply using more training data.

The proposed dynamic video synthesis and hard-negative contrastive objectives are technically plausible and individually supported by ablations. The paper is well organized, visually clear, and communicates the motivation effectively.
weaknesses: The central claim—adaptation to changing anomaly definitions—is not evaluated systematically. The quantitative experiments use each dataset's ordinary class-based definition and therefore primarily measure cross-dataset zero-shot generalization. Only two qualitative examples test counterfactual relabeling of the same event. A benchmark varying definitions while holding videos fixed, with frame-level quantitative results, is necessary to validate the main contribution.

The formal concept-drift argument is incomplete. The decomposition of P(Y|V) is an identity, but the assertion that drift is caused by P(Z|V) assumes without justification that P(Y|V,Z) is invariant. Moreover, a user-specified definition is better modeled as a conditioning variable or intervention than as a latent variable distributed according to P(Z|V). Consequently, the claim that the method 'avoids concept drift' is stronger than the analysis establishes.

The language-guidance ablation changes the placement of the fusion module and thus does not isolate dependence on language. There are no tests with mismatched prompts, paraphrases, exclusions, negations, compositional definitions, unseen concepts, or adversarial/ambiguous wording. The results therefore do not establish that predictions reliably follow the supplied definition rather than dataset or category priors.

Dataset quality and leakage controls are insufficiently documented in the main paper. The foundation-model filtering pipeline lacks audited precision, annotator counts, agreement measures, and error analysis. Because videos are gathered from public web and video-text sources, explicit near-duplicate checks against all seven evaluation datasets are essential.

Baseline comparisons are only partly controlled: many methods use different training data, several table entries are missing, and prompts are manually designed without a sensitivity analysis. Table 4 also averages AP on XD-Violence with AUC on other datasets, producing a summary number with unclear statistical meaning. No confidence intervals, multiple-run variation, or significance tests are reported.

Reproducibility is currently limited because code and data are only promised, while many implementation, annotation, and baseline-reproduction details are deferred to unavailable supplementary material.

The work provides no substantive ethics or governance discussion despite collecting surveillance, traffic-camera, and web videos involving violence and identifiable people. Privacy, consent, licensing/copyright, demographic bias, harmful surveillance applications, and dataset access safeguards should be addressed. Overall, the paper has strong potential, but the missing direct quantitative validation of its defining claim places it slightly below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The language-conditioned formulation addresses an important practical limitation of conventional video anomaly detection: what counts as anomalous can depend on a user's current policy or scenario.
PreVAD is potentially a valuable contribution: it is substantially larger and more diverse than standard VAD datasets and includes hierarchical categories and textual anomaly descriptions.
The empirical study is broad, covering seven cross-dataset test sets, two task protocols, temporal localization, classification, component ablations, prompt variants, and qualitative examples.
Comparisons against VadCLIP trained on the same PreVAD data help separate the effects of the proposed architecture from those of the much larger training dataset.

LaGoVAD consistently improves over the same-data VadCLIP baseline, while remaining feasible to train on a single RTX 4090. The supplementary material provides useful architecture and hyperparameter details.
weaknesses: The central concept-drift claim is not convincingly validated. Protocol 2 synthetically changes labels by selecting subsets of existing categories on only two datasets; it does not evaluate realistic policy changes, compositional definitions, negation, paraphrases, ambiguity, or definitions outside the training taxonomy. Five fixed subsets provide weak statistical coverage, with no confidence intervals or multiple-seed results.

The paper does not show that predictions are causally controlled by the supplied definition rather than primarily by category recognition. Essential controls are missing, such as irrelevant, contradictory, permuted, incomplete, and paraphrased prompts; per-definition results; and comparison to a simple CLIP category-recognition-and-masking baseline.

The probabilistic account is overstated. Treating a user policy Z as P(Z|V) is questionable because policy is normally externally specified, and conditioning on Z does not by itself 'avoid concept drift.' More importantly, training appears to retain a fixed mapping from each anomaly category to abnormality rather than exposing the same visual pattern to conflicting definitions, leaving a mismatch between Eq. 4 and the claimed behavior.

Dynamic video synthesis uses an abnormal source video's entire inserted interval as positive even though the training data have only video-level labels and the anomaly may occupy a small fraction of that source video. Thus, the claimed known pseudo-label positions are not actually known at frame level. The pseudo-label loss also omits an explicit negative-frame cross-entropy term, and concatenated clips may introduce artificial boundaries that make localization easier.

The zero-shot results have a serious unresolved contamination risk. PreVAD draws from large web/video datasets and RWF-2000, while the test benchmarks also contain web, movie, surveillance, and traffic footage. Independence from named VAD datasets does not establish media independence; no URL-, hash-, or near-duplicate audit is reported.

Dataset quality claims are insufficiently supported. There is no quantitative audit of category-label or generated-description accuracy, no inter-annotator agreement, no temporal-label agreement statistics, and no evaluation of hallucinations or demographic/source biases. A handful of examples cannot establish annotation quality at this scale.

Several comparisons are not fully controlled because LaGoVAD is trained on 35,279 videos while many cited methods use much smaller UCF/XD sets. The same-data VadCLIP comparison helps, but additional capacity-matched language-conditioned baselines are needed. The very low UCF macro-F1 also indicates weak or imbalanced category performance despite the reported accuracy.

Evaluation details introduce further uncertainty: manually designed prompts are not fully reported, test-time normalization on DoTA is underspecified, multi-label/co-occurring events can make category-subset relabeling incorrect, and hyperparameters appear selected using only limited reported validation evidence.

Reproducibility is limited by the promise to release only annotations and download scripts for mutable web content. Exact splits, prompts, preprocessing code, checkpoints, duplicate filtering, and stable access to the underlying videos are necessary to reproduce the headline results.

The ethics statement is inadequate. Public availability does not eliminate privacy, consent, copyright, licensing, or misuse concerns for surveillance footage and videos of violence, accidents, victims, and children. The authors also assert redistribution restrictions despite relying on third-party media, without documenting source licenses, takedown procedures, anonymization, or safeguards.

strengths: The paper targets a practically relevant limitation of conventional video anomaly detection by allowing the anomaly definition to be supplied in natural language at inference time.

PreVAD is substantially larger and more diverse than most existing VAD datasets, with a hierarchical taxonomy, anomaly descriptions, and unusually detailed disclosure of its data sources and curation pipeline.
The empirical study has broad coverage: seven cross-dataset benchmarks, a definition-shift protocol, a same-data VadCLIP comparison, component and hyperparameter ablations, and qualitative examples.
The method is computationally accessible, and the appendix provides useful architecture, optimization, and data-pipeline details.
weaknesses: The central framing is technically imprecise. A user-provided definition is an observed task condition, not naturally a random variable distributed as P(Z|V); conditioning on it does not by itself 'avoid concept drift.' The stability assumptions needed for P(Y|V,Z) are neither stated nor tested, and Eq. 3 inconsistently includes z in a model described as mapping only V to Y.

The main concept-drift evidence is too limited. Protocol 1 primarily measures ordinary cross-dataset generalization and confounds definition changes with domain, category, and feature-distribution shifts. Protocol 2 covers only two datasets and five hand-selected category subsets, rather than diverse free-form definitions, exclusions, negation, paraphrases, compositional rules, or genuinely novel user concepts.

Protocol 2 may contain label ambiguity: videos assigned to an excluded category are treated as normal even though datasets such as XD-Violence can contain multiple co-occurring anomalies. The paper does not describe relabeling or auditing temporal annotations under each definition, so the definition-dependent ground truth may be noisy or internally inconsistent.

Baseline fairness and reporting are unclear. Protocol-2 training data are not identified in Table 4; several competitors cannot condition their detector on a definition and therefore do not directly address the proposed task; reproduced LLM boundary outputs are converted to binary frame scores in an unfavorable manner; and proposed-model prompting appears manually designed without a controlled prompt-robustness study. The claim of surpassing alternatives across all datasets is also overstated, since LaGoVAD has lower UCF F1 than VadCLIP trained on PreVAD.

The zero-shot claims lack a credible contamination audit. PreVAD draws extensively from large web/video-text collections and public video platforms, while several test benchmarks also originate from web videos or movies. No URL-, hash-, or visual-near-duplicate checking against the seven test sets is reported. Hyperparameter tables also report UCF and XD test performance, raising concern that target benchmarks influenced model selection.

Dataset quality is asserted rather than established. AI-generated descriptions are not subjected to a reported human accuracy audit; category and temporal annotations lack agreement statistics; filtering thresholds and rejection/error rates are largely absent; and there is no analysis of hallucinations, label noise, class/source shortcuts, or description leakage from the same videos used for training.

Dynamic video synthesis assigns the entire weakly labeled abnormal source clip a positive pseudo-label, although the anomalous frames within that clip are unknown. Thus the statement that abnormal positions are known after synthesis is misleading. The resulting loss omits a negative-frame cross-entropy term and may reinforce noisy labels, while concatenation boundaries can introduce artificial temporal cues; no ablation rules out these shortcuts.

Several important empirical safeguards are missing: repeated runs or uncertainty estimates, statistical significance, matched-data/matched-compute comparisons beyond one backbone, systematic prompt sensitivity, and evaluation of whether performance actually changes correctly when only the definition changes. Averaging AP and AUC across datasets into a single detection score is also difficult to interpret.

The ethical discussion is inadequate for a surveillance dataset containing violence, crime, public streams, and identifiable people. Public availability does not eliminate privacy, consent, copyright, demographic-bias, or harmful-deployment concerns, yet the paper simply declares that no ethical issues exist. These omissions are especially concerning given the proposed real-world surveillance use.

strengths: The paper identifies an important limitation of conventional video anomaly detection: what counts as anomalous can change with the user's policy or context. Conditioning detection on a natural-language anomaly definition is a clear, practically relevant contribution.

PreVAD is a substantial dataset contribution, containing 35,279 videos across 35 subcategories, with hierarchical labels and anomaly descriptions. Its scale and domain diversity are valuable for studying cross-domain generalization.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering seven external datasets in a zero-shot setting. LaGoVAD consistently outperforms the strongest same-data comparison, VadCLIP trained on PreVAD, which provides concrete evidence that the proposed architecture contributes beyond dataset scale alone.

The concept-drift protocol directly tests changes in which categories are treated as anomalous, and LaGoVAD outperforms both multimodal VAD and general-purpose vision-language baselines on XD-Violence and MSAD.

The component ablations support the utility of language guidance, dynamic video synthesis, and negative-mining contrastive learning. Implementation details and hyperparameter ablations are reasonably comprehensive, and training is feasible on a single RTX 4090.
weaknesses: Protocol 2 evaluates only two datasets, five category subsets, and manually designed prompts. This tests category-set relabeling rather than the full claimed space of arbitrary user definitions; prompt paraphrases, negation, compositional definitions, and genuinely fine-grained policy changes are not systematically evaluated.

The dataset-quality evidence is insufficient for such a central contribution. Human annotators assign categories, but descriptions are generated by an MLLM, and the paper reports no quantitative audit of description accuracy, curation precision/recall, inter-annotator agreement, or temporal-label agreement.

Potential train-test contamination is not convincingly excluded. PreVAD aggregates public web videos and several large video-text datasets, while multiple evaluation benchmarks also contain web and movie footage. Avoiding direct ingestion of the named VAD datasets does not establish clip-level independence; perceptual deduplication against every test set is needed.

Baseline comparability is imperfect: Table 2 mixes published and reproduced results, most baselines use substantially smaller or different training sets, and only VadCLIP receives the controlled PreVAD training comparison. The conversion of boundary predictions from large VLMs into binary frame scores may also disadvantage those baselines.

The formal claim that conditioning on Z 'avoids concept drift' is stronger than established. It requires the conditional mapping P(Y|V,Z) to remain stable and training data to cover sufficiently varied definitions, assumptions that are neither clearly stated nor empirically stress-tested.

Dynamic synthesis treats the abnormal anchor's full temporal extent as anomalous despite having only video-level training labels, introducing pseudo-label noise. Equation 10 also lacks a complementary penalty for pseudo-labeled normal frames, so the characterization as temporal supervised learning needs clarification.
The reported UCF-Crime multi-class F1 is only 16.64 despite 51.72% accuracy, indicating weak class-balanced performance. Results also lack confidence intervals or variation across training runs.

The ethics and licensing discussion is inadequate. Public accessibility does not eliminate privacy, consent, copyright, or harmful-content concerns, particularly for surveillance and violent footage; the claimed absence of ethical issues and the proposed redistribution restrictions require a much more careful treatment.
